## Setup

```{python}
import pandas as pd

url = 'https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/banana_index.csv'
df = pd.read_csv(url, index_col='entity')
df.shape
```

```{python}
df = df.drop(['year', 'Banana values', 'type', 'Chart?', 'Unnamed: 16'], axis='columns')
df.columns.tolist()
```

## Part 1: Get your bearings

**1. How many foods are in the dataset, and how many columns are left after the drop?**

```{python}
df.shape
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**160 foods and 11 columns.** The file arrived with 16 columns and you dropped 5, so 11 remain.
The number of rows never changed, because dropping columns does not remove foods.
:::

**2. Display the first few rows. What do the three columns whose names begin with `Bananas
index` contain?**

```{python}
df.head()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
Each one is a **ratio**, not a measurement. Each column divides a food's climate cost by the
climate cost of the same amount of banana, and the three columns differ only in what "the same
amount" means: a kilogram of food, a thousand calories of food, or a hundred grams of protein. So a score of 20 means twenty
bananas' worth, on whichever basis that column uses. The raw emissions columns those ratios were
built from are still in the table, which is what lets you check the arithmetic yourself.
:::

**3. Run `.info()`. Two columns have missing values. Which, and how many?**

```{python}
df.info()
```

```{python}
df.isnull().sum()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**`emissions_100g_protein` and `Land use per 100 grams of protein`, two missing values each.**

Both are per-protein measures, and that is not a coincidence. A food with no protein at all
cannot have a per-protein figure, because the division has nothing to divide by. The missing
values are telling you something true about the food rather than something careless about the
data collection. A null is sometimes a fact, and this one is worth pausing on.
:::

**4. What is the value of `Bananas index (kg)` for `Bananas` itself? Explain in a sentence why
the number has to come out that way.**

```{python}
df.loc['Bananas', 'Bananas index (kg)']
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**1.0**, and it could not be anything else. The index is each food's emissions divided by the
banana's emissions, so the banana's own row is its emissions divided by itself. The banana is
the unit of the scale, in the same way that a metre is one metre long.
:::

## Part 2: Three rankings

**5, 6 and 7. The three top-10 lists.**

```{python}
df['Bananas index (kg)'].sort_values(ascending=False).head(10)
```

```{python}
df['Bananas index (1000 kcalories)'].sort_values(ascending=False).head(10)
```

```{python}
df['Bananas index (100g protein)'].sort_values(ascending=False).head(10)
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
Three lists of ten foods each, and the only thing that changed between them is the column name.
By kilogram the top ten is four beef products, three lamb, two cheeses and prawns. Per thousand
calories the beef stays at the top and lettuce, raspberries and coconut milk join it. Per
hundred grams of protein coconut milk, sugar and grapes take the first three places while beef
steak, beef mince and beef meatballs hold fourth, sixth and tenth.

If your numbers match but your row order differs, check that you passed `ascending=False`. If
you got a table with eleven columns rather than a single labelled column, you used the
whole-table form of the top-N pattern, which is not wrong but is harder to read here.
:::

**8. In a markdown cell, describe in two or three sentences how the three lists differ. Which
foods are near the top of all three? Which appear on only one, and can you say why?**

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
Ranked **per kilogram**, the list is meat: four beef products, three lamb, two cheeses and
prawns. Ranked **per thousand calories**, the beef stays but lamb largely drops out and lettuce
and raspberries appear, because they are mostly water and you have to eat a great deal of either
to obtain a thousand calories. Ranked **per hundred grams of protein**, three foods with almost no
protein in them take the top places: coconut milk, sugar and grapes, because dividing by a
number close to zero blows the ratio up. The beef does not leave, though. Beef steak is still
fourth, beef mince sixth and beef meatballs tenth, so the protein ranking mixes the genuinely
costly foods together with the arithmetic artefacts.

Beef is near the top of all three lists, which is the one robust finding. Sugar appears only in the
protein ranking, and the reason is arithmetic rather than agriculture: it is the denominator
approaching zero, not the numerator being large.
:::

## Part 3: Which foods are on every list?

**9. Print the three top-10 lists again, one after another, and compare them by eye. Write down,
in a markdown cell, the foods that appear in **all three**.**

```{python}
print('Top 10 for Bananas index (kg):')
print(df['Bananas index (kg)'].sort_values(ascending=False).head(10))

print('\nTop 10 for Bananas index (1000 kcalories):')
print(df['Bananas index (1000 kcalories)'].sort_values(ascending=False).head(10))

print('\nTop 10 for Bananas index (100g protein):')
print(df['Bananas index (100g protein)'].sort_values(ascending=False).head(10))
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Beef steak, Beef mince and Beef meatballs.** Those three, and nothing else, survive all three
ways of asking the question.
:::

**10. In a markdown cell: what does it mean for a food to be near the top of all three lists at
once? What would it mean for a food to top one list and appear on neither of the others? Name
one food of each kind.**

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
A food at the top of all three lists is expensive **however you measure it**. Its ranking does not
depend on the choice of denominator, so no reasonable objection about the basis of comparison
rescues it. **Beef steak** is the clearest case: first by weight, first by calorie, fourth by
protein.

A food that tops one list only is telling you about the **denominator**, not about the food.
**Sugar** is second per hundred grams of protein and appears nowhere else, because sugar has
essentially no protein, and a small number divided by a number close to zero is large. The
arithmetic behind the ranking is correct, but the claim it seems to make about sugar's climate
cost is misleading.

The practical lesson is that the choice of denominator is an argument, not a technicality. Pick
the one that matches what the food is actually for. Compare protein sources per gram of protein
and staples per calorie.
:::

## Part 4: Filtering by score

**11. Use the filter pattern to find every food with a `Bananas index (kg)` above 10. How many
are there?**

```{python}
expensive_by_weight = df[df['Bananas index (kg)'] > 10]
expensive_by_weight.shape
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**34 foods**, which is a little over one fifth of the dataset.
:::

**12 and 13. The `~` version, the `< 1` version, and why they differ.**

```{python}
no_worse_than_banana = df[~(df['Bananas index (kg)'] > 1)]
print(no_worse_than_banana.shape)

better_than_banana = df[df['Bananas index (kg)'] < 1]
print(better_than_banana.shape)
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**26 and 25.** The difference is exactly one row, and it is **Bananas itself**.

`~(df['Bananas index (kg)'] > 1)` keeps every food that is *not* above 1, which includes foods
that equal 1. `df['Bananas index (kg)'] < 1` is strictly less than, so it drops them. Only one
food in this dataset scores exactly 1.0, and by construction it is the banana.

The general point is that `~(x > 1)` means `x <= 1`, not `x < 1`. Negating a strict comparison
gives you a non-strict one, and the boundary value moves from one side to the other. Whenever a
filter returns one row more or fewer than you expected, check the boundary first.
:::

**14. Use a two-condition filter to find the foods that score above 5 per kilogram and below 1
per 100 g of protein. End the line with `.copy()`, because you will display the result a couple
of different ways. Display the two banana index columns for those foods, ranked by `Bananas
index (kg)`.**

```{python}
costly_but_protein_rich = df[
    (df['Bananas index (kg)'] > 5) & (df['Bananas index (100g protein)'] < 1)
].copy()

print(costly_but_protein_rich.shape)

costly_but_protein_rich[
    ['Bananas index (kg)', 'Bananas index (100g protein)']
].sort_values('Bananas index (kg)', ascending=False)
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**16 foods.** The `.copy()` matters because you display the result twice, once as a count and
once as a two-column ranking, and pandas warns you about editing a slice of another table if you
skip it.

Note the parentheses. Each condition is wrapped in its own pair before `&` joins them, and
leaving them out gives you an error about ambiguous truth values rather than the answer.
Question 15 asks what these 16 foods have in common, so read the row labels before you go on.
:::

**15. In a markdown cell: what do the foods in question 14 have in common? What is the argument
this table makes about how we should compare foods?**

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**16 foods, and almost all of them are animal protein**: fish (tuna, cod, cod fish fingers,
cod fishcakes, salmon, mackerel), poultry (chicken breast, thighs, wings, sausages, burger),
pork chops, pork sausages, eggs, and halloumi. Olive oil is the one that does not fit, and the
reason is worth chasing down. Its `Bananas index (100g protein)` is exactly `0.0`, and its
`emissions_100g_protein` is one of the two missing values you found in question 3. The zero is
standing in for a number nobody could compute, because olive oil has essentially no protein to
divide by, so olive oil met your `< 1` condition without ever being measured. Sunflower oil is
the other `0.0` in that column. A filter cannot tell a real zero from a missing one, and this is
the first time in the course that the difference has changed an answer.

The argument is this: these foods look costly when you weigh them and cheap when you weigh what
you eat them **for**. Nobody eats 100 g of chicken as a substitute for 100 g of lettuce; they eat
it as a source of protein. Comparing per kilogram flatters foods that are mostly water and
penalises foods that are dense in the thing you actually want. Choosing a denominator is choosing
what question you are asking, and this table is what that choice looks like when it changes the
answer.
:::

## Part 5: Land, not carbon

**16, 17 and 18.**

```{python}
banana_land_use = df.loc['Bananas', 'land_use_1000kcal']
banana_land_use
```

```{python}
df['land_use_1000kcal'].sort_values(ascending=False).head(10)
```

```{python}
hungriest = df['land_use_1000kcal'].idxmax()
print(hungriest)
print(df.loc[hungriest, 'land_use_1000kcal'] / df.loc['Bananas', 'land_use_1000kcal'])
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
A banana uses **2.72 square metres** of land per thousand calories. The most land-hungry food is
**beef steak**, at 223.7 square metres per thousand calories, which is **82.3 times** the
banana's land use.

Note that `.idxmax()` gave you the **label** and not the number. Returning the label is the
whole reason `.idxmax()` exists: paired with `.loc[]`, it lets you ask "which one?" and then
"how much?" as two separate, readable steps.
:::

**19. Compare your land-use top 10 with your emissions top 10 from question 6. Both are measured
per thousand calories, so they are the fair comparison. Are they the same foods? Answer in a
markdown cell, and name one food that appears on one list and not the other.**

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Seven of the ten foods are the same**: beef steak, beef mince, beef meatballs, beef burger,
cottage cheese, lamb (leg) and lettuce. So the two measures agree far more than they disagree,
and beef sits at the top of both.

Three foods appear only in the land-use list: **lentils**, lamb chops and chilli con carne.
Lentils are the interesting one. They take a lot of land per calorie and emit comparatively
little, so a ranking built on carbon alone would tell you nothing about them. Three foods appear
only in the emissions list: prawns, raspberries and coconut milk. Prawns are the mirror image,
because much of their footprint comes from fuel and refrigeration rather than from land.

Both lists here are per thousand calories, which is what makes the comparison fair. Had you
compared the land-use list against your question 5 ranking, which is per kilogram, some of the
difference you found would have been the change of denominator rather than a difference between
land and carbon.

Land and carbon are correlated but not interchangeable. A food can be costly in one and
unremarkable in the other, and which you measure determines which foods you notice.
:::

## Part 6: Cheese

**20. Build a table of just the cheeses, then find the cheese with the highest
`Bananas index (1000 kcalories)`.**

```{python}
cheese = df.filter(like='heese', axis='rows')
print(cheese.shape)

cheese['Bananas index (1000 kcalories)'].sort_values(ascending=False)
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Cottage cheese, at 33.51.** It is far above the rest: the next cheese, mozzarella, is 7.72,
so cottage cheese is more than four times the second-place figure. Cottage cheese is largely
water, so a thousand calories of it is a great deal of cheese.
:::

**21. How many rows did `.filter(like='heese')` give you? Look at the names carefully. Is every
one of them a cheese? In a markdown cell, say what the result tells you about matching rows on
text.**

```{python}
cheese.index.tolist()
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**12 rows, and no, they are not all cheeses.** `Cheesecake` and `Chocolate cheesecake` are
desserts, and `Macaroni cheese` is a cooked dish rather than a cheese. Only nine of the twelve
are cheese in the sense you meant.

Matching on a substring matches **strings, not meanings**. `.filter(like='heese')` did exactly
what you asked and had no way to know what you intended. Printing the labels and reading them is why you
read them after any text-based selection, rather than trusting the row count. The habit of
looking at what a filter caught, and not just how much it caught, will save you repeatedly.
:::

**22. Where does the top cheese sit in the whole dataset's calorie ranking? Check it against
your answer to question 6.**

```{python}
df['Bananas index (1000 kcalories)'].sort_values(ascending=False).head(10)
```

:::{.callout-note title="✅ Answer"}
**Fourth out of 160**, behind beef steak, beef mince and beef meatballs. It is visible in your
question 6 answer, which is the check: cottage cheese was already sitting in that top 10, and
finding it again from the cheese table means both calculations agree.

Cottage cheese is the only non-meat food in the top four of the calorie ranking, which is what
makes the cheese section worth having.
:::

## Part 7: Write it up

There is no single right answer here. A strong response cites at least three numbers you
computed, names at least one disagreement between the rankings, and reaches a conclusion the
numbers support. Here is one that would earn full marks.

:::{.callout-note title="✅ A model answer"}
Cutting bananas is not where the gains are. A banana scores 1.0 on the kilogram index by
definition, and it sits at 135th of 160 foods on that ranking. Beef steak scores 148.6 on the
same scale, so a kilogram of steak emits roughly 149 times what a kilogram of bananas emits, and
per thousand calories beef steak needs 82.3 times the land a banana needs. Removing bananas from
a diet changes a very small number and creates a gap that has to be filled by something else.

The dataset does make bananas look worse under one measure. Per hundred grams of protein they
rise to 63rd of 160, above eggs, chicken breast, salmon, tuna, cod and pork chops, because a
banana has almost no protein and the division inflates the ratio. The disagreement between the rankings is the point rather than a flaw. Coconut milk,
sugar and grapes top the protein ranking for the same arithmetic reason, and nobody would argue
that sugar is a worse climate choice than beef. The comparison is only meaningful when the
denominator matches what the food is for, and bananas are not a protein source.

If my friend wants a change that shows up in the numbers, the place to look is the 34 foods
scoring above 10 per kilogram, which is a little over a fifth of this dataset and is dominated by
beef, lamb and cheese. Substituting one of those a week would move more carbon than
eliminating bananas entirely.
:::
